## Residual RL and distillation back into the generalist

Residual RL adds a learned correction to a fixed controller <Cite id="residual-rl-2018" />. PLD (Probe, Learn, Distill; Xiao et al., 2025) freezes a VLA, trains task-specific residual actors with off-policy RL, lets them recover from the states the base policy reaches, and distills the trajectories back into the generalist through SFT. Residual exploration carries no safety guarantee <Cite id="pld-2026" />.

<Image id="pld-gpu-insertion-2025" />

On LIBERO, averages are 99.2% for the model labelled OpenVLA against 91.8% for its baseline, and 97.2% against 93.4% for π0. On a four-task SimplerEnv suite, Octo-SFT rises from 71.8% to 96.6% and the WidowX carrot task from 43.3% to 93.9%; the printed average delta is +24.9, though the means differ by 24.8 <Cite id="pld-2026" />.

On a Franka, PLD records 30/30 randomized trials for cube pick-up and peg insertion, but 28/30 for a blue cube and 20/30 for a red one under changed clutter. On YAM, four GPU insertion and removal stages distill into one BC policy that runs at least an hour continuously with recovery, though per-stage one-shot success stays below 100% <Cite id="pld-2026" />.

RLDG (Xu et al., 2024) uses HIL-SERL specialists to generate data for fine-tuning OpenVLA and Octo, so the generalist never receives RL updates. In FMB single-object assembly, RL supplies insertion data while humans supply grasping and transport, and OpenVLA succeeds in 20/20 trials against 12/20 with human demonstrations <Cite id="rldg-2024" />. Relabeling suggests action quality, more than state distribution, drives the benefit; the method needs task rewards, speed-optimized RL data can cause premature object drops, and OpenVLA commands actions at 4 Hz while RL runs at 10 Hz <Cite id="rldg-2024" />.

## EXPO-FT: value-guided edits on a frontier VLA

EXPO (Perry Dong, Qiyang Li, Dorsa Sadigh and Chelsea Finn; ICLR 2026) trains a large flow or diffusion base policy with a stable imitation objective plus a lightweight Gaussian edit policy that nudges sampled actions toward higher value, avoiding gradients through the denoising chain, and reports up to 2 to 3× better sample efficiency on average <Cite id="expo-2025" />.

EXPO-FT, from Dong, Kuo-Han Hung, Tian Gao, Sadigh and Finn, extends EXPO to VLA action chunks and human teleoperation corrections on π0.5. Tasks the base cannot do zero-shot get imitation fine-tuning to around 40% success or above before online RL, and sparse binary rewards come from rule-based detectors over 95% accurate. It reports 30/30 on every evaluated task within an average of 19.1 minutes of online robot data across eight task variants <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" />.

<ExpoFtResults className="my-6" />

The paper calls HIL-SERL highly reliable in its original evaluations; this suite randomizes a much larger initial-state space, and the standard budget was too small for learning to start on Cube Pick and Pool Shot. With extra samples, HIL-SERL reaches 27/30 and 13/30 there <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" /> <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" />.

DSRL keeps the base policy frozen and runs RL over its latent-noise space <Cite id="dsrl-2025" />. Dong and Finn argue it has a ceiling: "If the skill a robot needs isn't already somewhere in what the base model learned during pretraining, no amount of noise-searching will produce the action ...". DSRL averages 19/30 in their comparison <Cite id="perry-dong-post-training-2026" /> <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" />. PrefPI repeatedly fits preference-conditioned policies on self-generated trajectories, then amplifies the preference signal through classifier-free guidance <Cite id="prefpi-2026" />.

<NoiseOrEdit className="my-6" />

Dong and Finn's September 2026 blog post says: "RL shows incredible promise in training frontier robotics models, but it is not yet a recipe. It's a craft." EXPO-FT still needs a human to define success, reset the scene and intervene, longer horizons strain the value function, and "Nineteen minutes of robot interaction is not nineteen minutes of post-training," because gradient updates dominate wall-clock time <Cite id="perry-dong-post-training-2026" />. Real-Time EXPO-FT lets a lightweight edit policy react to the latest observation while a slow VLA proposes chunks, and on four dynamic real tasks average performance rises from 42% to 97% <Cite id="realtime-expo-ft-2026" />; [real-time execution](/manipulation/realtime-execution/) covers the latency budgets.

A review of robotic deep RL case studies lists real-world challenges that research on games and simulated control seldom addresses <Cite id="ibarz-2021" />, and a 2025 survey of real-world successes calls stable, sample-efficient real-world RL a priority <Cite id="tang-drl-survey-2025" />.

## Two ways to spend a transition

An <Term id="on-policy">on-policy</Term> method can only update on data the current policy generated, so each batch is collected, consumed and discarded; PPO allows several minibatch epochs per batch, where plain policy gradient takes one step <Cite id="ppo-2017" />. An <Term id="off-policy">off-policy</Term> method improves one policy from data another produced, so experience accumulates in a <Term id="replay-buffer">replay buffer</Term>. Underneath is <Term id="q-learning">Q-learning</Term>: fit the value of a state-action pair and bootstrap from the best next action, even one never taken <Cite id="sutton-barto-2018" />.

<ReplayReuse className="my-6" />

TD3 reduced DDPG's overestimation bias with clipped double critics, delayed policy updates and target policy smoothing <Cite id="td3-2018" />. DDPG itself is a model-free actor-critic built around deterministic policy gradients for continuous actions <Cite id="ddpg-2016" />. Soft actor-critic added a maximum-entropy objective aimed at sample complexity and brittle convergence <Cite id="sac-2018" />.

### Why robotics defaulted to PPO anyway

With thousands of GPU environments, steps are nearly free and training stability is the scarce resource. SAC's authors credit on-policy training with stability at the price of "poor sample complexity", and call off-policy learning with neural function approximation "a major challenge for stability and convergence" <Cite id="sac-2018" />.

<Image id="isaac-gym-allegro-envs-2021" />

Rudin and colleagues trained ANYmal with 4,096 parallel robots, 98,304 steps per update and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on one workstation GPU, more than 122,880 environment steps per second <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Minitaur's 160,000 control steps over about two hours average about 22 per second, below its 50 Hz rollout rate because resets and overhead count <Cite id="haarnoja-walk-2019" />. [Parallel simulation](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl) covers the first regime.

Most GPU-simulation work used PPO for its simplicity and ease of scaling, while off-policy methods were more data-efficient but slower in wall-clock time; Parallel Q-Learning scales to tens of thousands of environments and beats PPO in wall-clock time <Cite id="pql-2023" />, and FastSAC and FastTD3 train sim-to-real humanoid locomotion in 15 minutes on one RTX 4090 <Cite id="seo-2025" />.

edits.before:
<Term id="sample-efficiency">Sample efficiency</Term> is how much experience a method needs to learn. Haarnoja and colleagues learned Minitaur locomotion from 160,000 control steps in about two hours of real-world time that includes resets and the operator <Cite id="haarnoja-walk-2019" />. DayDreamer trained a Unitree A1 to roll over, stand and walk in one hour without a simulator, and ten more minutes of online learning taught it to withstand pushes; the authors intervened manually at the edge of the training area <Cite id="daydreamer-2022" />. A Walk in the Park demonstrates model-free quadruped learning directly on indoor and outdoor terrain with a carefully tuned controller <Cite id="walk-in-the-park-2022" />.

QT-Opt collected over 580,000 grasp attempts across seven robots in about 800 robot hours <Cite id="qt-opt-2018" />. The 2016 hand-eye preprint, which trained a supervised grasp-success predictor, reports about 800,000 grasp attempts over two months with 6 to 14 robots at a time <Cite id="levine-hand-eye-2016" />.

## Offline reinforcement learning

<Term id="offline-reinforcement-learning">Offline reinforcement learning</Term> learns a policy from a fixed dataset of transitions without further environment interaction during training, then deploys it <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />. It can reuse corpora like those in the [datasets module](/data-hardware/datasets), but a learned policy can choose actions outside the behavior distribution, Bellman targets then use erroneously high Q-values for them, and later backups propagate the errors without fresh feedback <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />. BCQ showed that this extrapolation error leaves standard off-policy algorithms unable to learn from fixed batches <Cite id="bcq-2018" />, and CQL answers it by learning a lower bound on policy value, penalizing Q-values on out-of-distribution actions <Cite id="cql-2020" />.

### Does any of this beat behavior cloning on robot data?

Mandlekar and colleagues found batch RL weak on human demonstrations: neither BCQ nor CQL did well on human datasets, while history-dependent BC-RNN was a strong baseline <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />. Kumar, Hong, Singh and Levine give sufficient conditions under which offline RL beats BC, assuming coverage of the optimal policy; with noisy data that improves coverage, conservative offline RL has a better bound than BC on equal expert data, while on expert data similar performance is a worst-case result. Their drawer-manipulation comparison, in simulation, pits BC on expert successes against CQL on noisy scripted data. Naive CQL can perform no better than BC <Cite id="offline-rl-vs-bc-2022" />.

For teleoperation data, a supervised [behavior-cloning baseline](/manipulation/bc-foundations) is the simpler starting point, though newer real-robot results favor RL. Generalist policies fine-tuned on RL-generated data beat the same policies trained on human demonstrations by up to 40% in success <Cite id="rldg-2024" />, and Physical Intelligence's RECAP pretrains a VLA with offline RL and more than doubles task throughput on some of the hardest tasks <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />.

## The reset problem

A simulated episode restarts from a fresh state automatically, at only computational cost <Cite id="autonomous-rl-2022" />; a physical one ends wherever the robot is, and a person or a learned behavior has to put it back <Cite id="leave-no-trace-2017" />.

Zhu and colleagues name learning from raw sensory inputs, assigning rewards without hand-designed instrumentation, and learning without human episode resets as the requirements for real-world RL; their D'Claw hand trained unattended, but evaluation included manual resets for bead manipulation <Cite id="real-world-rl-ingredients-2020" />. Leave No Trace learns a reset policy alongside the forward policy and aborts before non-reversible states <Cite id="leave-no-trace-2017" />. VaPRL learns to reach curriculum-selected starting states, reducing manual resets in simulated robotics tasks <Cite id="vaprl-2021" />. Sharma and colleagues' EARL benchmark sums gaps to optimal deployment return over training and treats interventions as constrained costs, though its experiments still schedule resets during training <Cite id="autonomous-rl-2022" />.

<Term id="reset-free-learning">Reset-free learning</Term> replaces manual resets with learned recovery behaviors. Gupta and colleagues' MTRF sequences task-specific policies with a designer-provided task graph, and a D'Hand on a Sawyer arm learned valve reorientation and pipe insertion without manual episode resets. The setup still used supplied rewards, motion capture for the in-hand object, scripted arm motion for pickup and a user who positioned the objects, pipe insertion used frozen fingers, and the method assumes that successful upstream tasks leave valid starting states for downstream ones <Cite id="reset-free-rl-2021" />. Without such a task graph a person handles the reset, a cost the human-in-the-loop line pays deliberately <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" />.

## Where this goes from here

[Parallel simulation](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl) explains the sampler behind on-policy training, [why RL won locomotion](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) which problems simulation represents faithfully, and [sim-to-real transfer](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer) deployment. [RL fine-tuning](/manipulation/rl-finetuning) covers RL on pretrained vision-language-action policies: pi_RL applies online PPO to flow-based pi0 and pi0.5 policies, replacing flow-matching regression with a policy-gradient update <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />, and PLD fine-tunes a generalist on hybrid recovery data from residual specialists <Cite id="pld-2026" />.

HIL-SERL reports 100% success in 100 evaluation trials per task, except IKEA whole assembly at 10 of 10. Nearly all tasks took one to two and a half hours of real-world training and timing-belt assembly six, counting scripted motion, rollouts and intended stops <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" />. ReF-HIL also uses successful human experience to shape critic values while constraining updates outside learned human-action neighborhoods <Cite id="ref-hil-2026" />. DROID <Cite id="droid-2024" /> and Open X-Embodiment <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" /> supply large real-robot demonstration corpora, but both papers evaluate imitation policies, so offline RL on them needs reward labels the datasets do not define.

## Camera intrinsics

Intrinsics map pixels to rays through focal lengths, principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's method recovers them from a planar pattern at a few unknown orientations <Cite id="zhang-2000-calibration" />, and Kannala and Brandt's generic model covers wide-angle and fisheye lenses <Cite id="kannala-brandt-2006" />. Refit after any focus, resolution or crop change. AnyCalib estimates pixel rays from one image and fits several camera models to them, including pinhole and fisheye models; its formulation also handles cropped or stretched images <Cite id="anycalib-2025" />.

## Depth is a measurement model

Stereo depth error scales with the square of distance, and repetitive structures make matches ambiguous <Cite id="realsense-tuning-2026" />; the D400 datasheet adds saturation from specular reflections <Cite id="realsense-d400-datasheet-2026" />. Kinect random error grows from a few millimeters to about 4 cm at maximum range <Cite id="khoshelham-kinect-2012" />, and a joint depth-color calibration with a depth-distortion model beat the manufacturer's <Cite id="herrera-depth-color-2012" />.

Camera Depth Models uses RGB and raw sensor depth to predict corrected metric depth, with synthetic sensor noise used during training <Cite id="camera-depth-models-2025" />.

## Hand-eye calibration

Hand-eye calibration finds the gripper-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$ <Cite id="shiu-ahmad-1989" />, Tsai and Lenz solved it in about ${}100 + 64N$ arithmetic operations for $N$ robot stations <Cite id="tsai-lenz-1989" />, and Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions <Cite id="park-martin-1994" />. Daniilidis represents the motions with dual quaternions and solves rotation and translation together using singular value decomposition <Cite id="daniilidis-1999" />.

## π0: the action expert

π0 grafts a second transformer, the action expert of about 300M parameters, onto a pretrained <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term> initialized from PaliGemma; the backbone handles image and text tokens, and the expert's 50 action tokens attend into it at every layer through shared self-attention. Inputs are 2 or 3 RGB images, language and proprioceptive state, and the model predicts H = 50 actions, executing 16 per inference at 20 Hz on UR5e and Franka or 25 at 50 Hz on the other robots <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. PaliGemma itself couples a SigLIP vision encoder to a Gemma language model for transfer across vision-language tasks <Cite id="paligemma-2024" />.

Where [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/) denoises with a DDPM, π0 trains the expert with conditional flow matching on a straight path. Training samples noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, forms $A_t^\tau = \tau A_t + (1 - \tau)\varepsilon$, and regresses $v_\theta$ onto $u = A_t - \varepsilon$. Inference integrates from $\tau = 0$ to $\tau = 1$ in 10 forward-Euler steps, with the image-text-state prefix KV-cached once so each step recomputes only the action suffix <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Lipman et al. found optimal-transport paths more efficient than diffusion paths for training and sampling <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />.

PI says π0, π0-FAST and π0.5 executed chunks synchronously, waiting for inference after each one , which the RTC paper later compared with asynchronous execution on π0.5 . ## Why ten steps is enough A DDPM path curves through noise space, while rectified flow straightens paths so that coarse time steps simulate them accurately . Trained on a 10k-hour cross-embodied mixture, π0-FAST matches π0's generalist performance with up to five times fewer GPU hours. ## π0.6 and π*0.6: scaling and experience

The π0.6 model card, dated November 17, 2025, initializes the backbone from Gemma3 4B, gives the action expert about 860M parameters and keeps expert gradients out of the backbone. Without task-specific fine-tuning, π0.6 folds laundry reliably and fully assembles the box 20% of the time, tasks that previously needed fine-tuning to succeed at all <Cite id="pi06-model-card-2025" />. In PI's Robot Olympics, fine-tuned π0.6 averaged 52% success and 72% task progress, while a fine-tuned standard VLM without π0.6's robot pre-training had no successes and 9% progress <Cite id="pi-olympics-2025" />.

π*0.6 uses Recap to learn from demonstrations, expert teleoperation corrections and autonomous experience, with a language-conditioned value function whose advantage, against a task-dependent threshold, gives each action a binary improvement indicator; human corrections are forced positive, and evaluation samples with the positive indicator <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />. The report places this formulation closest to CFGRL <Cite id="cfgrl-2025" />, while outside groups find RL on flow-based π0 and π0.5 hard because flow matching makes action log-likelihoods intractable <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />. The companion blog's example is a bad portafilter grasp that causes a later insertion failure <Cite id="pistar06-blog-2025" />.

On a rig with two 6-DoF arms and 50 Hz joint-position control, on-robot experience more than doubles successful completions per hour for double-shot espresso and diverse laundry, tested on a button-up shirt, against offline RL plus demonstration fine-tuning. Failures fall by "about a factor of two" ("more than 2×" in the figure), the "90%+" summary excludes diverse laundry, and the box task reports stages separately, with remaining failures mostly in final placement <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />.

In PI's February 2026 partner report, Weave describes π0.6 folding laundry at a customer laundromat, while Ultra describes live order packing with a human intervention system that also collects training data <Cite id="pi-partner-2026" />.

PI published MEM on March 3, 2026 <Cite id="mem-blog-2026" />. π0.6-MEM pairs a video encoder with a high-level policy that predicts updated natural-language summaries of earlier events, and handles tasks needing up to fifteen minutes of memory, such as recipe setup and kitchen cleanup. Its adaptation experiments train memory and memoryless policies on the same corrections, such as which way to open a refrigerator <Cite id="mem-2026" />.

The context holds task and subtask language, with the subtask from a learned high-level policy or a human, and episode metadata on quality, speed and mistakes; training uses different subsets of this context but always keeps the joint or end-effector control-mode label. Multi-view subgoal images come from a BAGEL-initialized world model, and subgoal and subtask generation run in separate threads <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. BAGEL is a unified decoder-only model pretrained on trillions of interleaved tokens <Cite id="bagel-2025" />.

π0.7 folds laundry on a bimanual UR5e with no laundry data for that robot, matching the task progress of experienced teleoperators trying it there for the first time <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. In the air-fryer example, language coaching fine-tunes a high-level policy that generates the subtasks without new teleoperation, which the authors call "early signs of compositional task generalization" <Cite id="pi07-blog-2026" />. [Human video](/manipulation/cross-embodiment/) joins the line through π0.5 co-fine-tuning, which roughly doubles performance on scenarios seen only in human data <Cite id="pi-human-to-robot-2025" />.

## Orbital robotics: servicing and removal

<Term id="on-orbit-servicing">On-orbit servicing</Term> covers satellite repair, refuelling, upgrades and debris removal <Cite id="space-manipulator-review-2025" />. It means matching a target's orbit, then docking with it or grasping it. An arm and its base satellite move each other, and in 1989 Umetani and Yoshida derived a generalized Jacobian from momentum conservation to control such arms <Cite id="umetani-yoshida-1989" />. A 2025 review organises capture control around free-floating and free-flying modes, from vision-based estimation to post-capture stabilisation <Cite id="space-manipulator-review-2025" />.

Relative navigation needs labelled spacecraft images. SPEED combines synthetic and real imagery for monocular pose estimation <Cite id="speed-challenge-2019" />; SPEED+ adds hardware-in-the-loop images with controlled poses and space-like illumination <Cite id="speedplus-2021" />. SPARK instead supplies simulated RGB and depth images labelled by spacecraft or debris class <Cite id="spark-2021" />.

The renderer has to reproduce the sensing problem. URSO uses Unreal Engine 4 to generate labelled views of spacecraft orbiting Earth <Cite id="urso-2019" />. SurRender's CPU ray tracer uses double precision to handle the scale difference between celestial distances and local target detail <Cite id="surrender-2021" />.

In 2020 Northrop Grumman's MEV-1 made the first docking of two commercial spacecraft in orbit, capturing Intelsat 901 in the graveyard orbit above geosynchronous altitude and returning it to service <Cite id="mev1-servicing-2025" />. After five years it undocked, the first such undocking in that orbit, and moved to its next mission <Cite id="mev1-servicing-2025" />. On July 21, 2026, Northrop Grumman's Mission Robotic Vehicle launched with the DARPA-funded RSGS payload, twin robotic arms built by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory <Cite id="rsgs-mrv-launch-2026" />. It will install small propulsion modules called mission extension pods to extend satellites' lives <Cite id="rsgs-mrv-launch-2026" />.

Debris is the uncooperative case, and ESA's 2026 report states that active debris removal is required to stop collisions multiplying debris <Cite id="esa-space-environment-2026" />. In 2024 Astroscale's ADRAS-J, flying for JAXA, inspected a discarded rocket upper stage in three fly-arounds and closed to about 15 m <Cite id="adras-j-15m-2024" />. No commercial spacecraft had come closer to debris, and the onboard collision-avoidance system aborted autonomously after an unexpected relative attitude anomaly <Cite id="adras-j-15m-2024" />.

By March 25, 2026, ADRAS-J had begun a controlled deorbit after 293 days in orbit <Cite id="adras-j-deorbit-2026" />. ADRAS-J2 targets launch in Japan's fiscal year 2027 to capture and remove an upper stage weighing about 3 t <Cite id="adras-j2-isar-2026" />.

NASA discontinued OSAM-1, a mission to refuel an unprepared satellite, in March 2024 after an independent review <Cite id="osam1-discontinued-2024" />. It cited technical, cost and schedule challenges and what it called a broader community evolution away from refuelling unprepared spacecraft, which left no committed partner <Cite id="osam1-discontinued-2024" />. In August 2026 NASA and Katalyst called off the LINK servicer's planned capture and boost of Swift, launched in 2004, over an attitude-control issue on the commercial spacecraft <Cite id="swift-boost-update-2026" />. NASA expected Swift to re-enter later in 2026 <Cite id="swift-boost-update-2026" />.

edits.before:
Learned control has flown on NASA's Astrobee free-flyers aboard the ISS. In 2025 Banerjee and colleagues reported the first in-space test of learned warm starts for trajectory optimization, while a convex solver still enforced safety <Cite id="banerjee-warm-starts-2025" />. The network cut solver iterations by 60 percent with rotational dynamics and 50 percent with in-distribution obstacles <Cite id="banerjee-warm-starts-2025" />. On May 27, 2025, the Naval Research Laboratory's APIARY team ran what it calls the first reinforcement-learning control of a free-flyer in space, with a policy trained in randomized simulation <Cite id="apiary-astrobee-2025" />.

The Space Robotics Bench authors say costly technology demonstrations and limited data severely hinder robot learning in space <Cite id="space-robotics-bench-2025" />. A September 2026 review adds space-specific dynamics and sensing, limited onboard resources and stringent safety requirements <Cite id="ai-space-robot-ops-review-2026" />. AI4MARS offers 326,000 crowdsourced terrain labels on 35,000 rover images, and a model trained on it exceeded 96 percent accuracy <Cite id="ai4mars-2021" />.

Space shares its [reliability](/frontier/reliability-gap/) bar with [surgical robotics](/adjacent/surgical/). Ingenuity flew more than fourteen times its five planned flights <Cite id="ingenuity-mission-end-2024" />, while OSAM-1 was cancelled before flight <Cite id="osam1-discontinued-2024" />. AEGIS and the digital-twin check on AI-planned drives both add autonomy in bounded, verified steps <Cite id="aegis-curiosity-2017" /><Cite id="perseverance-ai-drive-2026" />.

## Deformables and the long tail

A wooden block rests on one of six sides. A towel can be bunched up in more ways than any state estimator will ever enumerate, and some tasks add water, grease, or peanut butter <Cite id="holson-olympics-2025" />. Cloth, liquids, and compliant packaging fill Holson's task list: hang a dress shirt that starts with one sleeve inside out, clean peanut butter off your own manipulator.

Cloth manipulation depends on how the robot reduces the starting disorder. FlingBot learns a pick, stretch and fling primitive from visual observations <Cite id="flingbot-2021" />. SpeedFolding predicts paired gripper poses for bimanual actions, first smoothing the garment and then folding it along user-specified lines <Cite id="speedfolding-2022" />. Cloth Funnels chooses between flings and pick-and-place actions to bring garments into a canonical shape and aligned pose for later skills <Cite id="cloth-funnels-2022" />.

## Naive joint training

Fine-tuning a pretrained network through a random head distorts its features and raises out-of-distribution error <Cite id="kumar-finetuning-distorts-2022" />. The KI paper finds the same in VLAs: gradients from a new action expert degrade the backbone, slowing training and weakening language following, so that π0, told to bus a spoon into the bin, grasps trash <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

ChatVLA calls this spurious forgetting, robot training overwriting visual-text alignments <Cite id="chatvla-2025" />. Between robot tasks, though, pretrained VLAs resist forgetting, and simple experience replay sometimes removes it <Cite id="vla-continual-forgetting-2026" />.

## Limits and alternatives

Stopping expert gradients does not adapt the backbone: with the backbone frozen, the paper's shirt-folding policy scores 0%. FAST supervision supplies that signal, and vision-language co-training can give plain joint training good language following without stop-gradient <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

GR00T N1 freezes the language part of its VLM <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />. NVIDIA reports that N1.5, which froze the whole VLM among other changes, raised real GR-1 language following from 46.6% to 93.3% <Cite id="gr00t-n1-5-2025" />, and N1.6 unfreezes the top 4 layers <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />.

BLIP-2 bridges frozen image encoders and language models <Cite id="blip2-2023" />; VLM2VLA writes actions as language and trains only LoRA adapters <Cite id="vlm2vla-2025" />, and UAM keeps over 95% of its VLM's multimodal capability with no freezing, gradient stopping or co-training <Cite id="uam-forgetting-2026" />. Figure's Helix instead backpropagates from its fast policy into the VLM through their shared latent vector <Cite id="helix-2025" />, and HybridVLA trains discrete and diffusion action prediction together <Cite id="hybridvla-2025" />. InstructVLA jointly trains reasoning and action generation on vision-language and robot instruction data using mixture-of-experts adaptation <Cite id="instructvla-2025" />.

## Results

A many-embodiment π0 generalist needs 7.5 times the training steps of π0.5 + KI to reach similar table-bussing performance, and single-embodiment π0-FAST specialists need twice the wall-clock time from slow inference. Table bussing is scored at ten episodes per task and policy. When a mobile robot moves unseen objects into an open drawer, web-data co-training boosts generalization most, and language following improves but stays imperfect <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

In third-party fine-tuning, π0.5 with KI stays near zero on out-of-distribution task perturbations, so KI alone does not fix out-of-distribution language generalization <Cite id="apt-action-expert-pretraining-2026" />. A reimplemented co-training plus KI baseline trailed standard behavior cloning on mean LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-Plus success <Cite id="anchor-align-2026" />, though the dual FAST and flow objective mitigates forgetting more than flow alone <Cite id="garg-self-demonstrated-control-2026" />. Across seven VLAs, VQA co-training goes with better knowledge retention <Cite id="act2answer-2026" />, and in Toyota Research Institute's 89-policy study, training only on robot data cost the VLM backbone its ability to generate language <Cite id="lbm-cotraining-2026" />.

## A model can plan each step or train a policy in imagination

A planner rolls sampled action sequences through the model, executes the best first action and replans, so a new goal or cost needs no retraining, at the price of many rollouts per real step ([reward design and MPC](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc/)). In 2016 Finn and Levine combined action-conditioned video prediction with MPC so a real robot could push novel objects <Cite id="deep-visual-foresight-2016" />. TD-MPC2 trained one 317M-parameter agent on 80 tasks <Cite id="tdmpc2-2023" />, and PointWorld, trained on about 2 million trajectories, plans with MPC at 0.1 s per inference on a real Franka without demonstrations <Cite id="pointworld-2026" />.

Dreamer instead trains a policy on trajectories imagined in a learned latent space <Cite id="dreamer-2019" />, and DreamerV3 covers more than 150 tasks with one configuration <Cite id="dreamerv3-2023" />. Dreamer 4 learns purely offline, a setting its authors tie to robotics, where interaction "can be unsafe and slow" <Cite id="dreamer4-2025" />. [Latent dynamics](/world-models/latent-dynamics/) covers these agents.

<span id="when-to-choose-model-based-learning" />
## Model-based learning pays off when real interaction is expensive

It fits when interaction is expensive, goals change faster than dynamics and planning fits the latency budget; it fits less well when observations omit contact state or resets are cheap. Plan only once predicted action rankings track real ones: in a 2026 agile-driving study, SAC won in simulation, yet "only TD-MPC2 consistently outperforms the MPPI baseline on the physical platform" <Cite id="reset-free-driving-2026" />.

### Perception

Perception turns sensor streams into a model of the scene: which objects exist, where they are, how they move and what the road permits. Waymo's encoder fuses camera, lidar and radar inputs over time <Cite id="waymo-foundation-model-2025" />, and Waymo argues that no single sensor can replicate that redundant view <Cite id="waymo-ai-lessons-2026" />. BEVFormer, a camera-only bird's-eye-view detector, matched lidar-based baselines on the nuScenes test set <Cite id="bevformer-2022" />.

Point-cloud detectors make different choices about geometry. PointPillars organizes points into vertical columns for a 2D detector <Cite id="pointpillars-2018" />; PV-RCNN combines voxel convolutions with point-level features <Cite id="pv-rcnn-2019" />. CenterPoint detects object centres, estimates size, orientation and velocity, and links detections by nearest-centre matching <Cite id="centerpoint-2020" />.

Waymo's encoder fuses camera, lidar and radar inputs over time <Cite id="waymo-foundation-model-2025" />, and Waymo argues no single sensor can replicate that redundant view <Cite id="waymo-ai-lessons-2026" />. BEVFormer, a camera-only bird's-eye-view detector, matched lidar-based baselines on the nuScenes test set <Cite id="bevformer-2022" />.

Point-cloud detectors represent geometry differently. PointPillars organizes points into vertical columns for a 2D detector <Cite id="pointpillars-2018" />; PV-RCNN combines voxel convolutions with point-level features <Cite id="pv-rcnn-2019" />. CenterPoint detects object centres, estimates size, orientation and velocity, and links detections by nearest-centre matching <Cite id="centerpoint-2020" />.

<Image id="waymo-roof-sensor-suite-2025" />

edits.before:
### Prediction

Prediction estimates what every other agent will do over the next several seconds. The future is multi-modal: a pedestrian may cross or wait, and a predictor that averages the two forecasts a path through neither. The Waymo Open Motion Dataset made interactive forecasting a benchmark: over 100,000 scenes of 20 seconds at 10 Hz, more than 570 hours over 1,750 km of roads <Cite id="waymo-open-motion-2021" />.

Early predictors drew agent histories and map features into a top-down image for a convolutional network. VectorNet replaced that raster with a hierarchical graph network over vectorized polylines <Cite id="vectornet-2020" />. It matched or beat the raster with over 70 percent fewer parameters and an order of magnitude less computation <Cite id="vectornet-2020" />. MotionLM then cast multi-agent forecasting as language modeling over discrete motion tokens <Cite id="motionlm-2023" />.

A 2024 survey frames the trade: end-to-end systems optimize perception and planning features jointly, while modular designs are easier to interpret and debug <Cite id="e2e-ad-survey-2024" />. ### The measurement problem

Kalra and Paddock's 2016 RAND study found that test driving alone would need hundreds of millions of miles, sometimes hundreds of billions, to show safety <Cite id="kalra-paddock-2016" />. Mobileye's Responsibility-Sensitive Safety defines safe longitudinal and lateral distances as a white-box, interpretable model <Cite id="rss-2017" />. Its authors warned that without such standards the field risked a "winter of autonomous driving" <Cite id="rss-2017" />. Koopman argues that "safe enough" also requires no risk hot spots, such as reckless driving or risk shifted onto vulnerable populations, plus standards conformance and accountability <Cite id="koopman-safe-enough-2026" />.

Waymo's peer-reviewed 2025 study covered 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025 <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />. Against human benchmarks on the same roads, it found statistically significant lower rates of any-injury-reported, airbag-deployment and suspected-serious-injury crashes <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />. Vehicle-to-vehicle intersection crashes with any injury fell 96 percent, with no significant disbenefit in any of its 11 crash-type groups <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />.

Waymo's own safety hub reports 271.3 million rider-only miles through June 2026 <Cite id="waymo-safety-hub-2026" />. Over the same distance it counts 95 percent fewer serious-injury-or-worse crashes and 82 percent fewer injury-causing crashes than human drivers <Cite id="waymo-safety-hub-2026" />. IIHS found that Waymo's driverless vehicles in San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles and Austin had 68 percent fewer police-reportable crashes per mile than human drivers <Cite id="iihs-waymo-2026" />.

Tesla says it launched unsupervised rides in Miami, Orlando and Tampa in July 2026 and expanded its unsupervised area in Austin <Cite id="tesla-q2-2026-update" />. Baidu reported in August 2026 that Apollo Go had reached 28 cities and more than 240 million fully driverless kilometres <Cite id="baidu-q2-2026" />. Aurora began driverless customer deliveries between Dallas and Houston in May 2025 after closing its safety case <Cite id="aurora-driverless-launch-2025" />. By its count it drove nearly 440,000 driverless miles through June 2026 with zero collisions attributed to its system, and expected to end the year with 200 driverless trucks <Cite id="aurora-q2-2026" />.

## The relation to robot learning

The imitation toolkit was built on driving before it reached arms. DAgger, the canonical fix for covariate shift, was demonstrated on steering a car in a 3D racing game <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. It cuts the growth of mistakes over the horizon from quadratic to linear <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. On 500,000 hours of driving, Waymo found that forecasting and planning improve as a power law in compute, and closed-loop metrics improve too <Cite id="waymo-scaling-laws-2025" />.

RAD trains end-to-end policies by reinforcement learning in photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting replicas, to address imitation's causal confusion and open-loop gap <Cite id="rad-2025" />. It reports a 3x lower collision rate <Cite id="rad-2025" />.

EMMA is a vision-language model co-trained as a generalist on planning, detection and road-graph tasks, with its driving outputs written as text <Cite id="emma-2024" />. It is a <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action model</Term> whose embodiment is a car. A late-2025 survey splits driving VLAs into end-to-end models, which perceive, reason and plan in one network, and dual-system models, where a slow VLM deliberates over fast, safety-critical execution <Cite id="vla-ad-survey-2026" />.

Waymo's foundation model uses such a "Think Fast and Think Slow" design, a sensor-fusion encoder for rapid reactions beside a driving VLM trained using Gemini <Cite id="waymo-foundation-model-2025" />. The split mirrors the end-to-end versus [hierarchical](/manipulation/hierarchical/) divide in manipulation and the [knowledge insulation](/manipulation/knowledge-insulation/) case for a separate fast path. NVIDIA reports that its Alpamayo-R1 driving VLA runs on the vehicle in real time at 99 ms latency <Cite id="alpamayo-r1-2025" />.

Shiva Sreeram, Daniela Rus and colleagues at MIT CSAIL and the University of Haifa (October 2026) asked six open video-language models which way the ego car moves in driving clips <Cite id="mind-temporal-gap-2026" />. On 200 simulated forward and 200 backward clips, every model answered forward every time, and the same biases appeared on 60 real videos <Cite id="mind-temporal-gap-2026" />. After LoRA finetuning on 80 percent of those clips, all six scored 100 percent on the held-out 80, and the authors conclude that the motion cues are learnable but not reliably exposed through prompting <Cite id="mind-temporal-gap-2026" />.

A redundant arm uses the pseudoinverse $J^{+} = J^{T}(JJ^{T})^{-1}$, whose spare freedom can serve goals such as avoiding joint limits <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />, ranked against the end-effector task in Siciliano and Slotine's task-priority framework <Cite id="siciliano-slotine-1991" />. Near singular points, Nakamura and Hanafusa's singularity-robust inverse returns a motion close to the desired path <Cite id="nakamura-hanafusa-1986" />.

Wampler's damped least-squares formulation makes the tradeoff explicit: reduce pose error while penalizing the size of the corrective joint motion <Cite id="wampler-1986" />.

## Inverse kinematics

Inverse kinematics seeks $q$ with $k(q) = x_d$ for a target $x_d$. The map is nonlinear: a reachable target can have several configurations, such as elbow left or right, a redundant arm has a continuum, and an unreachable target has none <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. Move the shoulder slider in the figure below to trace the hand's path, then drag the cup and watch the arm work out an angle for every joint.

Horizon separates the planned chunk length $H$, the <Term id="predicted-horizon">predicted horizon</Term>, from the steps executed before re-planning, the <Term id="committed-horizon">committed horizon</Term>. Diffusion Policy's simulated CNN Push-T reference uses observation, prediction and execution horizons of 2, 16 and 8 <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />; ACT's 100-step entry is its k=100 chunk-ablation reference <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />; OFT+ predicts and executes 25 actions at 25 Hz on ALOHA <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />; and π0.7 predicts 50 with five denoising steps and executes 15 or 25 <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. [Real-time chunking](/manipulation/realtime-execution/) generates the next chunk while the current one executes <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" />.

Control frequency needs a named measurement setting. ACT's ALOHA setup runs at 50 Hz with <Term id="temporal-ensembling">temporal ensembling</Term> <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />, RT-1 commands the Everyday Robots platform at 3 Hz <Cite id="rt1-2022" />, and RT-2's multi-TPU cloud service runs PaLI-X-55B at 1 to 3 Hz <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. Ha and Schmidhuber trained an agent "entirely inside of its own hallucinated dream" and transferred it back to the real environment <Cite id="ha-world-models-2018" />. DreamerV3's Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) pairs a recurrent state that carries memory with a stochastic categorical representation, and learns to reconstruct inputs and predict reward and continuation <Cite id="dreamerv3-2023" />.

Dream-MPC refines policy-proposed action sequences by gradient ascent on predicted return, with an uncertainty penalty. Used in place of MPPI in pretrained TD-MPC2 and BMPC on 24 simulated tasks, over three seeds and ten episodes, the BMPC variant raises interquartile mean by 26.7% and mean by 20.5%. The TD-MPC2 variant beats its policy alone but does not consistently match MPPI <Cite id="dream-mpc-2026" />. BMPC learns its policy by imitating the MPC planner <Cite id="bmpc-2025" />, and HumanoidBench, one of the three task suites, poses whole-body humanoid tasks <Cite id="humanoidbench-2024" />.

TD-M(PC)² found that planner-generated data causes "persistent value overestimation" and fixed it with a policy constraint, gaining most on 61-DoF humanoids <Cite id="td-m-pc2-2025" />. Fast-WAM, a video world-action model, keeps video co-training but encodes the current frame once and runs action denoising on a chunk, with success similar to its imagine-then-execute variants on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0. On Galaxea R1 Lite towel folding it reports 190 ms inference latency against 810 ms for Fast-WAM-IDM on one RTX 5090D V2 32GB GPU <Cite id="fast-wam-2026" />.

## TD-MPC2's authors expect broad generalization to need far more tasks

TD-MPC2's authors expect broad generalization, such as transfer to new embodiments, "will likely require several orders of magnitude more tasks" <Cite id="tdmpc2-2023" />. <Term id="cycle-time">Cycle time</Term> is the time required to produce a part or complete a process, measured for that operation <Cite id="lei-cycle-time-definition" />. <Term id="takt-time">Takt time</Term> is available production time divided by customer demand, and its purpose is to match production with demand <Cite id="lei-takt-time-definition" />. NASA distinguishes inherent availability, computed from <Term id="mean-time-between-failures">mean time between failures</Term> and mean time to repair without administrative, logistics or preventive-maintenance time, from operational availability, which includes them. Uptime is time in an operable state <Cite id="nasa-availability-prediction-analysis" />.

The calculator above reports capital cost per modeled pick: robot price times the integration multiple, divided by modeled lifetime picks over a fixed amortization period. It does not include running costs. The <Term id="payback-period">payback period</Term> is total system capital cost divided by monthly labour, reduced-damage and throughput value. EVST's guide estimates 12 to 24 months for multi-shift palletising cells and 24 to 36 months for single-shift or lower-throughput operations <Cite id="evst-cell-cost-2026" />.

## The jam rate is the lesson

A separate authored example has no measured intervention rate behind it. At 99 percent per-pick success, with every failure needing a ten-second clearing, overhead is (1 − 0.99) × 10 = 0.1 seconds per attempted pick. Amazon's stow system is designed to stow 80 percent of warehouse items at 300 units per hour. A no-stow turnaway, when a pod leaves with nothing stowed, consumes at least 12 seconds <Cite id="amazon-stow-2025" />.

The <Term id="intervention-rate">intervention rate</Term> and clearing cost together decide whether a cell ships. Physical Intelligence reports that training on deployment data, including expert corrections during autonomous runs, more than doubled throughput and roughly halved the failure rate on some of its hardest tasks <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />. Ken Goldberg proposes combining model-based engineering with model-free learning so robots can perform useful work, collect real-world data, and use those data to improve performance and learn adjacent skills. Goldberg does not claim that engineering removes the need for learning, and he expects model-free AI eventually to enable fully general-purpose robots <Cite id="goldberg-data-gap-2025" />.

[The Reliability Gap](/frontier/reliability-gap) tracks the demo-to-production gap and selected deployment examples; [Autonomous Vehicles](/adjacent/autonomous-vehicles) covers the same question for driverless cars. Morgan Stanley's 2026 note on the humanoid industry's "PR problem", as reported by CNBC, describes [investors](/market-map) looking for real-world return on investment over polished demonstrations <Cite id="morgan-stanley-pr-problem-2026" />. Figure says its livestreamed logistics run lasted 200 hours <Cite id="helix-2-5-2026" />, but it was one task at one site, with [no published success rate](/data-hardware/evaluation-crisis).

## The labour evidence, disagreement intact

Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo find that one more robot per thousand workers cuts the US employment-to-population ratio by about 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42 percent. Losses concentrate in commuting zones exposed to industrial automation <Cite id="acemoglu-restrepo-2020" />.

In Germany, robot-driven displacement in manufacturing was fully offset by new jobs in services, and the cost fell mostly on young workers entering the labour force <Cite id="dauth-robots-germany-2021" />. Spanish manufacturers that adopted robots raised output by 20 to 25 percent within four years and created net jobs at a rate of 10 percent <Cite id="koch-robots-firms-2021" />. French adopters also grew employment, at their competitors' expense, and the overall effect on industry employment was negative <Cite id="acemoglu-lelarge-restrepo-2020" />.

## Scaling has early laws, such as EgoScale's log-linear fit to validation loss

The claim: keep the architecture general, scale data and parameters, and generalist robot intelligence follows, as it did for language. Rich Sutton's 2019 essay The Bitter Lesson frames it: general methods that leverage computation win in the long run <Cite id="sutton-bitter-lesson-2019" />. Brooks answered six days later, in a reply that paraphrases Sutton and describes itself, including its closing comment, as "seventy six words shorter than Sutton's post" <Cite id="brooks-better-lesson-2019" />. Bessemer's investor analysis argues that "scaling laws are emerging" and that capital is the moat <Cite id="bessemer-robotics-2026" /> ([VLA models](/manipulation/vla-models/)).

EgoScale fit a log-linear <Term id="scaling-law">scaling law</Term> (R² = 0.9983) from human-video pretraining hours to validation loss, which it reports correlates strongly with downstream robot performance <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />. Its full recipe lifts average success by 54% over a no-pretraining baseline on a 22-DoF hand <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />. Figure reports a human-to-humanoid transfer law on robot-action prediction, with Index pretraining lifting zero-shot success in 30 unseen homes from 9% to 56% <Cite id="helix-2-5-2026" />. Lin et al. found single-task success following "a roughly power-law relationship with the number of environments and objects" <Cite id="lin-data-scaling-laws-2024" />. In entirely new homes, π0.5 cleaned kitchens and bedrooms <Cite id="pi05-2025" />.

## Skild AI

Skild AI's January 14, 2026 [Series C](/market-map/) raised \$1.4 billion at a valuation of over \$14 billion. Skild calls its model "omni-bodied", names simulation and Internet video for pretraining and teleoperation and deployments for post-training, and says the model can control robots without prior knowledge of their body form. That announcement gives no architecture, parameter count, control rate, chunk horizon, benchmark protocol or weight terms <Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" />.

Skild's July 2025 technical note describes a hierarchy: a slower policy for manipulation and navigation feeds a faster policy that produces joint angles and motor torques <Cite id="skild-brain-2025" />.

A September 2025 post describes training on 100,000 simulated robots <Cite id="skild-omni-bodied-2025" />. Skild presents S1 (August 18, 2026) as an in-context learner: shown a video of a task, it executes it, and on unseen long-horizon tasks of 4 to 8 minutes Skild reports 66% cumulative per-step success, against 9% for language prompting <Cite id="skild-s1-2026" />. The company also reports passing \$100M in annual recurring revenue <Cite id="skild-arr-2026" />.

## Generalist AI

Generalist AI says GEN-0 (November 2025) is pretrained on over 270,000 hours of [real-world manipulation data](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck/), growing by 10,000 hours a week <Cite id="generalist-gen0-2025" />. <ExplainerFigure id="flying" />

Simulation separates what the camera sees from how the airframe moves. Flightmare decouples rendering and dynamics so they can run independently <Cite id="flightmare-2020" />. FlightGoggles can feed rendered sensor measurements to a physical vehicle flying in a motion-capture room <Cite id="flightgoggles-2019" />. AirSim combines Unreal Engine rendering with physics and hardware-in-the-loop interfaces <Cite id="airsim-2017" />.

Classical stacks plan a trajectory and then track it. Mellinger and Kumar generated minimum-snap trajectories for quadrotors <Cite id="mellinger-minimum-snap-2011" />, and Lee and colleagues built a geometric tracking controller on SE(3) <Cite id="lee-se3-control-2010" />. In 2021 time-optimal trajectory planning outperformed professional human pilots in racing <Cite id="foehn-time-optimal-2021" />.

Wind adaptation adds a separate learned component. Neural-Fly learns a shared aerodynamic representation offline, then adjusts a small set of mixing coefficients online as conditions change <Cite id="neural-fly-2022" />.

Swift, from the University of Zurich, raced three human champions, including the world champions of two leagues, and won several races against each <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. It trained its control policy in simulation with model-free reinforcement learning <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. The team then fitted residual models of perception noise and unmodeled dynamics from real flight data and retrained <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />.

In September 2023, Song and colleagues showed that an RL controller outperformed optimal control on the same racing task <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. Optimal control splits the problem into planning and control with a trajectory as the interface, which limits the controller under unmodeled effects. RL optimizes a task-level objective directly and handles model uncertainty through domain randomization; it flew above 12 g and 108 km/h <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. A later hybrid embedded a differentiable MPC in an actor-critic framework and matched model-free RL at up to 21 m/s <Cite id="ac-mpc-2026" />.

In April 2025 a TU Delft drone with one rolling-shutter camera and an IMU won the A2RL race in Abu Dhabi, beating all AI teams and three human world champions in a knockout tournament <Cite id="monorace-2026" />. TU Delft notes that Swift raced in a lab where the researchers controlled conditions, hardware and track, while the A2RL organisers designed both hardware and track <Cite id="tudelft-a2rl-2025" />.

In January 2026 world FPV champion Minchan Kim beat TII Racing's drone from a 4 to 4 tie when it struck a gate and could not recover <Cite id="a2rl-2026-final" />. Champion policies stay narrow: they often crash immediately in unseen configurations, and a 2026 method improved generalization 7.4x <Cite id="green-generalization-2026" />.

## The autonomy stack on a flying robot

One camera and one low-cost IMU are the minimum sensor suite for metric six-DoF state estimation <Cite id="vins-mono-2018" />. <Term id="visual-inertial-odometry">Visual-inertial odometry</Term> fuses image features with IMU measurements into the pose and velocity the controller needs, without GPS or motion capture <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. ## What the rest of robotics takes from it

Latency budgets transfer directly. A policy that infers at 20 Hz controls a contact-rich task at about 20 Hz whatever the arm's bandwidth, the reasoning the perception-latency study formalised for flight <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />. [Real-time execution](/manipulation/realtime-execution/) covers that budget for manipulators.

The sim-to-real recipe also carries over: residual models fitted from real data <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" /> plus privileged imitation with realistic sensor noise <Cite id="high-speed-flight-2021" />. [Sim-to-real transfer](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer/) and [parallel simulation](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl/) cover it for other robots.

Champion claims need context. Swift won in its own lab and MonoRace on organiser hardware <Cite id="tudelft-a2rl-2025" />, and the 2026 final turned on one unrecovered gate strike <Cite id="a2rl-2026-final" />. The distance between peak and reliable performance is the [reliability gap](/frontier/reliability-gap/), and [surgical robotics](/adjacent/surgical/) shows a bar cleared under regulatory oversight.

The mean moves through the true maps $g$ and $h$; only the covariance takes the linearized route <Cite id="thrun-2005" />. The Ames group moved from linearizing about a nominal reference trajectory to relinearizing about the *current estimated state*, which they hoped would bring "substantial advantages". An accidentally off-nominal simulation converged after initial overshoots, and the report names this modification the extended Kalman filter. ## DROID: depth on one platform

DROID's distinction is scene and site diversity: 76,000 trajectories totaling 350 hours, across 564 scenes and 86 tasks, gathered by 50 operators at 13 institutions over 12 months <Cite id="droid-2024" />. Every trajectory came from one rig, a Franka Panda with two ZED 2 cameras and a ZED Mini wrist camera, [teleoperated](/data-hardware/teleop-rigs) through a Meta Quest 2. One platform gives one action space and one camera geometry, at the price of embodiment lock-in.

Single-platform collections can be larger. RT-1's fleet of 13 robots gathered about 130k episodes over 17 months <Cite id="rt1-2022" />, and Language-Table released nearly 600,000 language-labelled trajectories <Cite id="language-table-2022" />. The Galaxea Open-World Dataset holds 500 hours across 50 scenes, all from one consistent robot embodiment <Cite id="galaxea-open-world-2025" />.

<Term id="diffusion-policy">Diffusion policies</Term> trained on DROID beat policies trained on the next-best dataset by 22% in-distribution and 17% out-of-distribution <Cite id="droid-2024" />. The project added language annotations for 75,000 episodes in December 2024 and improved camera calibrations for 36,000 in April 2025 <Cite id="droid-project-page" />. The paper releases DROID under CC BY 4.0 <Cite id="droid-2024" />, whose deed allows commercial sharing and adaptation subject to attribution, a license link, change notices and the other license terms, and warns that other rights may limit a particular use <Cite id="cc-by-4-0-deed" />.

## How to read dataset claims

Hours compare better than episodes. DROID averages about 17 seconds per trajectory and AgiBot World Beta about 11, so a large episode count can hide less interaction than a smaller set of long tasks ([the data bottleneck](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck)). The 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge supplies 10,000 teleoperated demonstrations totaling 1,200+ hours <Cite id="behavior-challenge-2025" />, and the synthetic InternData-A1 holds over 630k trajectories and 7,433 hours <Cite id="interndata-a1-2025" />.

Modalities differ as much as size. RH20T records visual, force, audio and action data in over 110,000 contact-rich sequences <Cite id="rh20t-2023" />. Humanoid Everyday adds depth, LiDAR and tactile streams to 10.3k humanoid trajectories across 260 tasks, with a cloud evaluation platform <Cite id="humanoid-everyday-2025" />. Scaling work finds task diversity worth more than per-task demonstration count, and multi-embodiment pretraining optional given high-quality single-embodiment data <Cite id="diversity-scaling-2025" />.

Hand-object datasets make contact supervision explicit. ContactDB uses thermal imaging to record grasp-contact maps <Cite id="contactdb-2019" />; ContactPose pairs contact with hand pose, object pose and RGB-D images <Cite id="contactpose-2020" />. DexYCB benchmarks hand and object pose estimation and safe robot grasps for human-to-robot handover <Cite id="dexycb-2021" />.

HOI4D supplies egocentric RGB-D video with hand-pose, object-pose and action annotations <Cite id="hoi4d-2022" />. OakInk connects object affordances to recorded human interactions and transfers those interactions to virtual counterparts <Cite id="oakink-2022" />.

Object models supply another kind of supervision. ShapeNet organizes CAD models by semantic category and records attributes such as alignment and size <Cite id="shapenet-2015" />. PartNet adds detailed hierarchical part labels <Cite id="partnet-2018" />; ABC retains explicitly parameterized curves and surfaces for geometric ground truth <Cite id="abc-models-2018" />. The YCB set pairs physical everyday objects with scans, physical properties, geometric models and example manipulation protocols <Cite id="ycb-models-2015" />.

## From dataset headline to training contract

A useful dataset is legal for the intended deployment, consistent in actions, units, frames and rates, complete for the claimed tasks, scenes and embodiments, and downloadable as versioned episodes traceable to a release. Datasheets for Datasets asks every dataset to document its motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses <Cite id="datasheets-for-datasets-2018" />. LeRobot's format moved to multi-episode files in 2025, after one file per episode hit file-system limits at millions of episodes <Cite id="lerobot-dataset-v3-2025" />.

Mixing datasets needs a canonical observation and action schema, one adapter per source and source labels kept through training, so positive transfer can be told apart from one corpus dominating <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" /> <Cite id="octo-2024" /> <Cite id="remix-2024" />. The [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack) supplies the versioned artifacts, and the [robot-learning roadmap](/manipulation/robot-learning-roadmap) places dataset selection in a broader program.

## They solve different specification problems

MuJoCo models articulated bodies, constraints and contact with explicit equations and parameters <Cite id="mujoco-2012" />. Isaac Lab wraps GPU simulation, sensors, task definitions and batched environments into a robot-learning workflow <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. Disney Research, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA gave their Newton GPU engine to the Linux Foundation in September 2025 <Cite id="newton-lf-2025" />. NVIDIA reports that MuJoCo Warp speeds up MJX by 252x on locomotion and 475x on manipulation on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU <Cite id="newton-manipulation-blog-2026" />.

A learned world model estimates transitions from observations and actions, often in a latent or video space, and trades parameter error for dataset and generalization error. Hansen and Wang call hallucination "inherently a data coverage issue" <Cite id="wm-hallucination-2026" />. A 2026 survey lists simulation among a world model's roles, with planning, policy learning, evaluation and data generation <Cite id="world-model-survey-2026" />.

Graph Network-based Simulators keep a particle representation but learn the update: particles are graph nodes and message passing predicts dynamics for fluids, rigid solids and deformable materials <Cite id="graph-network-simulator-2020" />.

## Clip generators run far slower than interactive world models

In the costlier video column, Cosmos Predict1 spans diffusion models at 7B to 14B and autoregressive models at 4B to 13B <Cite id="cosmos-predict-2025" />. NVIDIA measured Predict2's 14B Video2World at 56 GB of VRAM and about 85 seconds per 480p clip on a GB200, over 30 minutes on a DGX Spark <Cite id="cosmos-predict2-perf-2025" />. The Predict1 14B card lists over 80 GB for a five-second 1280x704 clip with the prompt upsampler offloaded <Cite id="cosmos-1-diffusion-14b-card-2025" />. Such offline clip generators cannot serve as 24 fps runtimes, and a policy calling one per action step inherits their latency.

DeepMind reports that Genie 3 runs at 24 fps and 720p <Cite id="genie-3-2025" />, and the Interactive World Simulator holds 15 FPS for over 10 minutes on one RTX 4090 <Cite id="interactive-world-simulator-2026" />. DreamZero controls a robot at 7 Hz from a 14B video model <Cite id="dreamzero-2026" />.

## Gaussian splats render in milliseconds but carry no dynamics

3D Gaussian Splatting renders rasterizable primitives in tens of milliseconds or less per frame, with no weights or tokens, and stores the scene as an asset of 1 to 5 million Gaussians <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />. A splat shows what a view looks like; physics must say what an action does.

<Image id="gaussian-splatting-garden-2023" />

<span id="where-learning-has-the-advantage" />
## Learning captures appearance and contact that are costly to model

A learned visual model can absorb from video the textures, reflections, cables and clutter that are expensive to render; deformable contacts, unmodeled actuators and wear also resist parameterization. Robotic World Model aims a neural simulator at policy optimization <Cite id="robotic-world-model-2025" />, and RoboWorld at policy evaluation, with task-progress scoring and rankings validated against real robots <Cite id="roboworld-2026" />.

<span id="three-hybrid-patterns" />
## Four hybrid patterns

### Learn appearance, keep dynamics

Real-to-sim systems reconstruct a scene's appearance and keep a physics engine for motion and contact, as RoboGSim does with Gaussian splatting <Cite id="robogsim-2024" />. SplatSim's splat-rendered simulator gave zero-shot RGB policies 86.25% success, against 97.5% when trained on real data <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. The pattern suits rigid-body tasks and is weaker for friction or tool compliance. PhysTwin extends it to deformables, building spring-mass twins of ropes, stuffed animals, cloth and delivery packages from videos and rendering them with Gaussian splats <Cite id="phystwin-2025" />. A separate soft-body evaluation framework reconstructs video-based twins and uses splat-rendered rollouts to assess policies for plush-toy packing and rope routing <Cite id="softbody-splat-eval-2025" />.

### Generate content, keep the engine

### Learn residual dynamics

Residual models start from explicit dynamics and learn the measured difference, such as actuator delay or contact impulses. ## Evaluation must use the same real anchor

Both simulator types can be wrong in correlated ways: a policy may exploit contact softness in physics or visual shortcuts in a world model. SIMPLER builds matched environments and correlates simulated with real policy performance <Cite id="simpler-2024" />. Apply that test to both types with several policy families and held-out environments, scored on the same real outcome ([world-model evaluation](/world-models/evaluation/)).

<Image id="isaac-lab-assembly-real-2025" />

<span id="a-selection-rule" />
## Choose by what can be specified and what the data cover

Use explicit physics when state and mechanics can be specified, counterfactuals are broad, constraints need inspection or parallel stepping matters most ([parallel simulation for RL](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl/)). Use a learned world model when real observations hold structure that is costly to author, data cover the decisions of interest and validation can anchor model error. Use a hybrid for a localized mismatch, as ANYmal's simulator did <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />; [classical control](/classical/control/) and [latent dynamics](/world-models/latent-dynamics/) cover the two ends.

## Multimodal demonstrations

When one operator passes an obstacle on the left and another on the right, mean-squared-error regression averages the demonstrations into a collision. Energy-based implicit policies often beat such explicit policies <Cite id="implicit-bc-2021" />, and diffusion models learn an expressive distribution over the joint action space <Cite id="pearce-diffusion-bc-2023" />. Pan et al. (2025) contest this motivation: generative policies owe their gains to supervised iterative computation, and a two-step regression policy essentially matches flow policies <Cite id="much-ado-noising-2025" />. Fine-tuned OpenVLA-OFT, an L1-regression VLA, beat from-scratch Diffusion Policy and ACT by up to 15 points of average success <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />.

## Denoising in action space

<DiffusionDenoising className="my-6" />

The policy is a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) <Cite id="ddpm-2020" /> conditioned on recent observations. Where a regression head computes $a_t = f_\theta(o_t)$, Diffusion Policy models $p(A_t \mid O_t)$ over the next $T_p$ actions. Inference starts from Gaussian noise and repeatedly subtracts a fraction of the noise that the denoiser $\epsilon_\theta$ predicts,

$$
A_t^{k-1} = \alpha \left( A_t^k - \gamma \, \epsilon_\theta(O_t, A_t^k, k) + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) \right)

## Cartesian actions

Cartesian actions say what the tool should do. Once range and frame are fixed, relative deltas from the current pose label arms with different joint counts and link lengths alike, provided each robot supplies inverse kinematics or an operational-space controller; Khatib's 1987 operational space formulation unifies motion and force control <Cite id="khatib-1987" />. Euler angles and quaternions are discontinuous as network outputs, while 6D representations are continuous <Cite id="rotation-continuity-2018" />.

GR00T N1.6's notes find relative actions smoother and more accurate than absolute ones but prone to error accumulation on small datasets <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />, and in matched VLA pretraining ablations a unified end-effector-relative representation was critical for cross-embodiment transfer <Cite id="vla-scaling-alignment-2026" />. X-VLA instead learns a separate set of soft-prompt embeddings for each data source as embodiment-specific prompts <Cite id="x-vla-2025" />.

## Torque and impedance actions

Torque actions expose dynamics and contact; Levine et al. mapped raw images to motor torques <Cite id="levine-visuomotor-2015" />. They need a high rate and a safety layer that holds when the output is wrong: libfranka sends 1 kHz commands in five modes, including gravity- and friction-compensated joint torque <Cite id="franka-fci-docs" />, while Rudin et al.'s locomotion pipeline sends joint-position targets to a PD controller <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

## Tokens change the output geometry

RT-2 <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> and OpenVLA map continuous actions to vocabulary tokens to reuse language-model training, OpenVLA binning seven dimensions into 256 values <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. Binning allows cross-entropy but limits resolution and adds autoregressive decoding to latency. BEAST encodes sequences as fixed-length B-spline tokens, allowing parallel decoding without separate tokenizer training <Cite id="beast-2025" />.

FAST compresses a chunk's frequency coefficients with byte-pair encoding, far better than per-dimension binning, and its universal FAST+ tokenizer was trained on 1M real robot action trajectories <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. ActionCodec evaluates tokenizers by optimization properties, including temporal overlap, vocabulary redundancy and token independence <Cite id="actioncodec-2026" />. VQ-BeT's vector-quantized actions infer 5 times faster than Diffusion Policy <Cite id="vq-bet-2024" />, and LAP writes end-effector motions as short natural-language phrases, with LAP-3B averaging over 50% zero-shot success on three unseen robots <Cite id="lap-2026" />.

## A selection rule

Choose the lowest-level action the task requires and the platform supports safely. Across 13,000+ real rollouts and 500+ models, predicting delta actions consistently helped, with joint space favoring control stability and task space favoring generalization <Cite id="action-space-design-2026" />. Hold controller, rate, horizon and observation history fixed when comparing architectures, or the comparison measures interface changes. In one vision-based sim-to-real study of picking and pushing, joint velocity beat the tested pose and joint-increment alternatives <Cite id="rl-action-spaces-2026" />.

## Domain randomization: train on a distribution of simulators

Jakobi and colleagues found in 1995 that sim-to-real correspondence depended on how much noise the simulation used <Cite id="jakobi-1995" />. Tobin and colleagues randomized textures, lighting and camera pose for tabletop object localization; their best network localized objects to about 1.5 cm over 480 webcam images of eight geometric objects, though most runs used ImageNet initialization (random initialization nearly matched it given enough simulated data), and their abstract frames the real world as "just another variation" once the simulator varies enough <Cite id="tobin-2017" />.

Peng and colleagues randomized link mass, joint damping, friction, controller gains, action timing and observation noise, maximizing expected return over [that dynamics distribution](/how-robots-work/#worlds). A recurrent policy trained only in simulation pushed a puck with a seven-DoF Fetch arm, with start and target positions randomized within a 30 cm square <Cite id="peng-2018" />. Chen and colleagues' analysis bounds the sim-to-real gap and highlights the importance of history-dependent policies <Cite id="chen-dr-theory-2021" />.

<Image id="mujoco-playground-franka-block-2025" />

## Teacher-student distillation: privilege in, proprioception out

Teacher-student training splits sensing from control: a teacher learns from privileged simulator state, then a student with deployable sensing imitates it. Learning by Cheating used this two-stage form for driving <Cite id="learning-by-cheating-2019" />, after asymmetric actor-critic had given only the critic full state <Cite id="asymmetric-ac-2017" />.

Lee and colleagues distilled a privileged RL teacher, which saw simulator-only terrain and contact information, into a temporal convolutional student via its actions and latent features. The student uses two seconds of <Term id="proprioception">proprioceptive</Term> history, plus the command and current state, and one controller per robot generation took ANYmal-B and ANYmal-C robots through mud, snow, rubble and vegetation without environment-specific tuning <Cite id="lee-2020" />. Isaac Lab's DextrAH-RGB example distills a privileged KUKA and Allegro teacher into a stereo-RGB network <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />, and VIRAL's authors report that scaling to tens of GPUs, up to 64, made teacher and student training reliable for an RGB humanoid that ran up to 54 loco-manipulation cycles <Cite id="viral-2025" />.

RMA trains a base policy and an environment-factor encoder jointly with RL, then regresses an adaptation module on simulated state-action histories to predict the latent extrinsics. The module reads 50 state-action steps (0.5 seconds) and updates asynchronously at about 10 Hz on the A1, while the base policy runs at 100 Hz on the latest estimate, with no online gradient updates. The paper reports adaptation in fractions of a second without real-world fine-tuning, and failures after large perturbations or multiple leg obstructions; its latent encodes behavior-relevant conditions without guaranteeing each physical parameter <Cite id="rma-2021" />. UP-OSI had earlier fed dynamics parameters predicted from recent history into a universal policy <Cite id="up-osi-2017" />.

Tan and colleagues paired an identified actuator model and simulated latency with randomization <Cite id="tan-quadruped-2018" />. SPI-Active samples parameters in parallel with Fisher-information-driven excitation and beats baselines by 42 to 63% in locomotion tasks <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />, and Miller and colleagues tune Spot simulation against hardware with CMA-ES <Cite id="miller-spot-2025" />. An Unsupervised Actuator Net fits complex actuation from real data without torque sensing, supporting athletic loco-manipulation transfer <Cite id="fey-athletic-2025" />.

ASAP pretrains phase-conditioned tracking policies in IsaacGym on <Term id="retargeting">retargeted</Term> human motions, runs them on a Unitree G1, and records trajectories with motion capture and onboard sensors. A second PPO policy learns a delta action added before the simulator step, the tracking policy is fine-tuned with the frozen delta model in simulation, and only the tracking policy is deployed. For the hardware study the delta covers only four ankle DoFs of the 23-DoF model <Cite id="asap-2025" />. HALO calibrates the unloaded robot first, then identifies an unknown payload's mass distribution with differentiable simulation <Cite id="halo-payload-2026" />.

Evaluation separates IsaacGym-to-IsaacSim and IsaacGym-to-Genesis tests, with open-loop replay and closed-loop tracking over 43 motion sequences, and ASAP does not win every metric: in the easy IsaacSim closed-loop group its mean global joint-position error is 106 mm against SysID's 105 mm. On hardware, compared only with Vanilla, the error falls from 61.2 to 50.2 mm on kicking and from 159 to 112 mm on LeBron James's "Silencer" <Cite id="asap-2025" />. ASAP reports better tracking on the held-out "Silencer" motion without establishing coverage of arbitrary unseen skills, and its stated hardware limits are motor overheating and damage, motion-capture dependence and the data needed for a full 23-DoF delta model <Cite id="asap-2025" />. Swift's champion-level drone racing likewise combined simulation RL with physical-world data <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />.

## Force limits rest on measured pain thresholds by body region

Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer and Hirzinger made the force question empirical with crash-test impacts <Cite id="haddadin-2009" />. Later pain-threshold studies, such as Han and colleagues' 37-subject impactor tests, report limits by body region and contact geometry <Cite id="han-force-pain-2024" />. A power-and-force-limited application therefore attaches a measured number to a named body part, the value the [contact-force lab in the control module](/classical/control/) also reads <Cite id="han-force-pain-2024" />.

<span id="the-stack-the-standards-actually-form" />
## Risk assessment comes first, and a compliant robot does not make a compliant cell

<Term id="risk-assessment">Risk assessment</Term> begins with ISO 12100, the general-principles standard for machinery safety, at edition 1 since 2010 and due to be replaced by a revision now in draft <Cite id="iso-12100" />. Its abstract describes the procedure: identify the hazards, estimate and evaluate the risks, then reduce them, documenting and verifying each step <Cite id="iso-12100" />. The reduction measures form a hierarchy: design the hazard out, guard against what remains, then inform the operator, the "3-step approach" OSHA's manual reproduces from the robot industry association <Cite id="osha-otm-robots" />.

The robot-specific layer splits liability in two. ISO 10218-1 covers the robot as partly completed machinery, the manufacturer's obligation; ISO 10218-2 covers the application and its cell, the integrator's <Cite id="iso-10218-1-2025" /> <Cite id="iso-10218-2-2025" />. Both were republished in February 2025 at editions 3 and 2, the first major revision since 2011. The US adoption, ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025, added a Part 3, approved on October 7, 2025, that gives guidance to users of industrial robot cells <Cite id="a3-r1506-2025-store" /> <Cite id="rr-ansi-r1506-2026" />.

<span id="the-humanoid-gap-and-the-standard-that-is-not-finished" />
### The humanoid standard is still a committee draft at stage 30.60

A humanoid falls, a hazard class the industrial documents were not written for. ISO/CD 25785-1 covers industrial mobile robots that need active control to remain balanced, including bipedal machines <Cite id="iso-cd-25785-1" />. It is a committee draft: the comment period closed on 8 July 2026, and in late October 2026 the catalogue still showed stage 30.60, with edition 1 unpublished and no date for the next stage <Cite id="iso-cd-25785-1" />. A parallel technical report for the United States and Canada, ANSI/A3 TR R15.108, is under development for dynamically stable industrial mobile robots including humanoids <Cite id="agility-digit-5-2026" />.

Until those documents are agreed, a humanoid deployed beside people runs under a risk assessment that invents its own treatment of fall risk. Agility reports that Digit 5 avoids people, stops or sits down under an independent safety controller, and that Digit passed an independent field evaluation on a customer production line against safety standards administered by OSHA <Cite id="agility-digit-5-2026" />. Brooks predicts that without new types of mechanical systems walking humanoids "will remain too unsafe to be in close proximity to real humans" <Cite id="brooks-scorecard-2026" />.
